core.text: 7 Limitations

TrajFusion leverages supervision signals from problems where model sampling yields both correct and incorrect trajectories, as such cases provide the most informative reasoning variations. Consequently, the strength of the supervision signal depends on the presence of sufficient outcome diversity during sampling, while questions that are consistently solved correctly or incorrectly offer limited contrastive information, in which case TrajFusion naturally reduces to vanilla rejection sampling fine-tuning behavior.
A.2 Trajectory Fusion
Construction.

For each query, we identify the set of incorrect responses generated during rejection sampling. These responses are grouped by their final extracted values, and we select the shortest representative from each group to prioritize concise reasoning paths with minimal redundancy.
Sequence Formatting.

A complete assistant reply is constructed by interleaving the selected incorrect responses with fixed reflective prompts, simulating a trial-and-error reasoning process. The sequence concludes with a correct solution followed by a positive feedback phrase and the final answer. The trajectory is encapsulated within a thinking block to provide structured supervision:
If no eligible incorrect completions are found, the sequence defaults to a standard format containing only the correct response within the <think> block, omitting the error and reflection components.
A.3 Training Setup
Framework and Resources.

We perform training using the ms-swift framework with DeepSpeed ZeRO-1 optimization. All models are trained on 8×\timesA100 80GB GPUs using bf16 mixed-precision and input sequence packing to improve efficiency.
Hyperparameters.
Table 4 provides the detailed training configurations for each base model. We evaluate models at fixed data intervals within the first epoch to monitor performance dynamics (Figure 3).

core.text: 3 Preliminaries
3.1 Semantic property in latent space

Next-token prediction creates a simple but revealing interface between discrete tokens and continuous hidden states. A token is read in through WinW_{\mathrm{in}}, transformed layer by layer into a latent representation, and then converted back to a distribution over the vocabulary through WoutW_{\mathrm{out}}. This makes it natural to describe what the model “means” by a token using objects that live in latent space.

Recent work on LM semantics (Gu et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2025) promotes a geometric viewpoint where each vocabulary label corresponds to a distinguished latent vector, so that tokens have explicit representatives inside the model. On the input side, these representatives are already visible, since each row of WinW_{\mathrm{in}} is how the model instantiates a token internally. On the output side, the LM head defines how hidden states are interpreted as vocabulary scores, and we can place output labels into the same latent-space coordinates by mapping them back through the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse.

Let VV be LM vocabulary size and dd the model dimension, with V≫dV\gg d. We denote the input embedding matrix by Win∈ℝV×dW_{\mathrm{in}}\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times d} and the unembedding matrix by Wout∈ℝd×VW_{\mathrm{out}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times V}. This yields two vocabulary-indexed collections of latent vectors

Bin\displaystyle B_{\mathrm{in}} =Win∈ℝV×d,\displaystyle=W_{\mathrm{in}}\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times d}, (1) Bout\displaystyle B_{\mathrm{out}} =Wout+∈ℝV×d,\displaystyle=W_{\mathrm{out}}^{+}\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times d}, (2)
where (⋅)+(\cdot)^{+} denotes the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse.

Figure 1 visualizes these collections as colored dots, one per vocabulary label, together with an arbitrary hidden state shown as a dark dot. The left panel shows the input-side perspective induced by BinB_{\mathrm{in}}. The right panel shows the output-side perspective induced by BoutB_{\mathrm{out}}, which is essentially the same linear readout used by LogitLens when it probes intermediate hidden states. When these two perspectives are not aligned, the same latent direction can correspond to different token meanings depending on whether we interpret it through the input interface or the output interface.

Given such vocabulary representatives, the scores of a hidden state can be understood geometrically as comparisons to all vocabulary anchors. One can view the pre-softmax scores as induced by distances or similarities between the hidden state and the anchor set. Numerically this recovers the standard matrix-multiplication logits, but the geometric language is helpful for understanding how emphasizing or suppressing a particular semantic meaning corresponds to moving a representation toward or away from specific anchors. In Figure 1, the dashed connections from the dark dot to colored dots depict these comparisons.

This geometry also provides a lens on the forward pass itself. Given a sequence t1,t2,…,tnt_{1},t_{2},\ldots,t_{n}, the model uses the last token tnt_{n} as the medium through which it predicts tn+1t_{n+1}. Let f0,f1,…,fmf_{0},f_{1},\ldots,f_{m} denote the hidden states of this medium token across an mm-layer transformer, where f0f_{0} is the embedding lookup and fmf_{m} is the final-layer representation used for prediction. As the representation flows through layers, its nearest or most compatible vocabulary anchors may change, yielding a layer-by-layer evolution of its implied meaning. We refer to this evolution as a semantic transition, and the sequence {fℓ}ℓ=0m\{f_{\ell}\}_{\ell=0}^{m} records a transition trace of how next-token prediction emerges through depth.
3.2 Token-interface consistency and weight tying

The geometric picture above depends not only on representations fℓf_{\ell}, but also on the token interface that defines the vocabulary anchors themselves. If the anchors used to read tokens in and the anchors used to read predictions out are synchronized, then token meanings are consistent across the model’s input and output boundaries. Algebraically, this synchronization corresponds to the input-side and output-side anchor sets agreeing, which can be expressed as Win≜Wout+W_{\mathrm{in}}\triangleq W_{\mathrm{out}}^{+}.

Figure 2 illustrates this process as a trajectory of the medium token across layers. By comparing each fℓf_{\ell} to the vocabulary anchors in the corresponding latent space, we can associate each layer with the token meaning that is most strongly supported at that depth. When the latent semantics are stable, this transition is smooth and interpretable. When the latent semantics drift, the same geometric neighborhood can correspond to different labels at different layers, making the transition appear erratic.

In practice, most language models parameterize WinW_{\mathrm{in}} and WoutW_{\mathrm{out}} independently, or tie them by a transpose. Transpose tying reduces parameters, but it does not in general enforce a pseudo-inverse relationship, and therefore does not guarantee that BinB_{\mathrm{in}} and BoutB_{\mathrm{out}} stay aligned. When this misalignment grows during pretraining, the model effectively uses one coordinate system to write tokens into the network and a slightly different one to read them out. Figure 2 shows how such a mismatch manifests across depth. Under transpose tying, the semantic geometry drifts from layer to layer, visualized as shifting color bands, and the medium token can appear to “change its nearest meaning” even when its trajectory is smooth in raw hidden-state space. In contrast, when the input and output interfaces are synchronized, the anchor set remains stable across layers, and the semantic transition of the medium token is measured against a consistent vocabulary geometry.

A seemingly direct remedy would periodically recompute a pseudoinverse with SVD and retie the matrices, but doing so is computationally expensive and can be numerically brittle at scale. Motivated by the token-interface viewpoint and the layerwise effects highlighted in Figure 2, we instead seek to maintain input–output semantic synchronization throughout training by enforcing a structural consistency condition at the interface itself
Wout​E≈Id,W_{\mathrm{out}}\,E\approx I_{d}, (3)

where E∈ℝV×dE\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times d} is the embedding and Wout∈ℝd×VW_{\mathrm{out}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times V} is the unembedding. The key goal is to achieve Eq. (3) by construction rather than by a soft regularizer, while keeping the method stable and practical for large-scale pretraining. This is the core motivation for Pseudo-Inverse Tying, which we introduce next.
4 Approach: Pseudo-Inverse Tying

We generalize standard weight tying into a shared-memory view: both embedding and unembedding are derived from a single shared token memory and two coupled (inverse) transforms. Concretely, we introduce a shared memory matrix Z∈ℝV×dZ\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times d} and an invertible transform T∈ℝd×dT\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}, and define
E=Z​T−1,Wout=T​Z⊤.E\;=\;Z\,T^{-1},\qquad W_{\mathrm{out}}\;=\;T\,Z^{\top}. (4)

Eq. (4) can be understood as pseudo-inverse tying via shared projection: ZZ stores token “semantic memories” (rows), while TT specifies a learnable change-of-metric (scaling & mixing) that is applied symmetrically to the input and output sides via T−1T^{-1} and TT.
If ZZ has orthonormal columns,
then the pseudo-inverse consistency holds exactly:
Therefore, PIT reduces the problem of maintaining Eq. (3) to two simple structural requirements: ZZ stays on the Stiefel manifold; TT is invertible (we will choose TT to be SPD).
4.1 Polar Decomposition for Shared Memory

In practice, we often start from an arbitrary tall matrix Z~∈ℝV×d\tilde{Z}\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times d} (e.g., a teacher embedding, or a random Gaussian initialization). To satisfy Eq. (5) in a numerically stable and canonical way, we use the thin polar decomposition:
Z~=U​H,U⊤​U=Id,H≻0.\tilde{Z}\;=\;U\,H,\qquad U^{\top}U=I_{d},\qquad H\succ 0. (7)
We then set the shared memory to the orthonormal factor:
Z←U.Z\leftarrow U. (8)

Polar decomposition is particularly convenient because it explicitly separates an orthonormal basis (UU) from a symmetric positive definite (SPD) scale/mixing component (HH), which aligns with our goal of disentangling a shared semantic memory from a learnable metric.

To satisfy actual needs, we design two working modes: (i) teacher-mode initializes all parameters from an existing pretrained checkpoint and enables PIT during continued pretraining. In this case, ZZ is initialized from a pretrained teacher embedding via polar decomposition; (ii) scratch-mode, initializes all parameters from scratch and trains with PIT enabled throughout. In this case, ZZ is initialized from random Gaussian followed by polar decomposition.
Initialization in teacher-mode

Let E0∈ℝV×dE_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times d} be the teacher embedding. We compute E0=U​HE_{0}=UH and set Z←UZ\leftarrow U. A simple practice is to initialize T←IT\leftarrow I and learn TT during training.
Initialization in scratch-mode
We sample Z~∼𝒩​(0,1)V×d\tilde{Z}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)^{V\times d} and compute its polar (or thin QR) factorization to obtain an orthonormal ZZ satisfying Eq. (5).
4.2 Full SPD Transform for Pseudo-Inverse Tying
Constraint on TT
We learn TT as a full symmetric positive definite matrix:
T≻0.T\succ 0. (9)

Choosing TT to be SPD ensures invertibility, improves numerical stability, and (critically) provides richer expressivity than diagonal or basis-diagonal scaling: a full SPD transform can represent both scaling and mixing through its eigenstructure.

Efficient Forward Computation

PIT does not require materializing EE and WoutW_{\mathrm{out}} as standalone parameters; instead, both are computed from (Z,T)(Z,T). Given hidden states h∈ℝB​T×dh\in\mathbb{R}^{BT\times d} (batch size BB, sequence length TT), logits are computed as
logits⁡(h)=h​Wout=h⁡(T​Z⊤).\mathrm{logits}(h)\;=\;h\,W_{\mathrm{out}}\;=\;h\,(TZ^{\top}). (11)

5 Experiments

We evaluate PIT under both pretraining and post-training updates. PIT constructs the embedding and unembedding as coupled projections of a shared token memory using an orthonormal memory Z∈ℝV×dZ\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times d} and a learned SPD transform T∈ℝd×dT\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}:
E=Z​T−1,Wout=T​Z⊤,E=ZT^{-1},\qquad W_{\text{out}}=TZ^{\top},

which guarantees a pseudo-inverse-consistent token interface (Wout​E=IdW_{\text{out}}E=I_{d}) whenever Z⊤​Z=IdZ^{\top}Z=I_{d} and TT is invertible. Our experiments are designed to answer three questions. (i) Does PIT improve training stability and convergence at fixed compute. (ii) Does it better preserve input-side vs. output-side semantics throughout training. (iii) Does this translate into more predictable performance under lightweight post-training updates.

For LM pretraining we report learning curves and summarize performance at fixed token budgets. For LM post-training updates, we additionally report semantic and interface diagnostics that are deterministic given a checkpoint.
5.1 Experimental Setups
Baselines
Unless stated otherwise, we compare standard transpose typing, shortened as TT against PIT.
Models

We evaluate with a family of openly released GPT LMs, Cerebras-GPT (Dey et al., 2023) at 111M, 256M, 590M, and 1.3B parameters. Compared with GPT-2 (Yenduri et al., 2023), Cerebras-GPT better fits our focus, including tied weighting and no-bias LM head, meanwhile all model layer follow same design. We also evaluate a group of models at 133M, 303M, 613M, and 1.17B parameters that we train from scratch, marked as Scratch. These models span on-device to edge-server scales and provide controlled settings to test whether interface constraints matter most during early optimization.
5.2 Implementation Details
Shared memory ZZ

PIT requires Z⊤​Z=IdZ^{\top}Z=I_{d}. In teacher-mode, we compute a thin polar decomposition of the teacher embedding matrix and take the orthonormal factor as ZZ. In scratch-mode, we initialize ZZ as a random Stiefel matrix. Unless otherwise noted, we freeze ZZ after initialization, so all interface adaptation happens through the learned SPD transform.
SPD transform TT

We parameterize T≻0T\succ 0 via a Cholesky factorization T=L​L⊤T=LL^{\top} with positive diagonal, where the diagonal is mapped by exp⁡(⋅)\exp(\cdot) to enforce positivity. We compute triangular solves in FP32 for numerical stability.
Efficient computation

We compute logits as (h​T)​Z⊤(hT)Z^{\top}, avoiding explicit formation of WoutW_{\text{out}}. For embedding lookup, we retrieve token rows ztz_{t} from ZZ and apply T−1T^{-1} via triangular solves instead of an explicit inverse. This preserves the intended pseudo-inverse relationship while keeping overhead close to standard tying.
5.3 Results on LM Pre-Training

We pretrain on FineWeb-Edu (Penedo et al., 2024). To fit the data needs of on-device LMs, we do experiments with the official 10B-token subset. We use checkpoint-native tokenizers in teacher-mode and a fixed tokenizer in scratch-mode. We train with AdamW on a fixed context length of 1K tokens, and apply gradient accumulation to reach a fixed global batch size.

For pretraining we report learning curves and summarize performance at fixed token budgets. Table 1 reports final perplexity after continued pretraining in teacher-mode or full pretraining in scratch-mode on FineWeb-Edu 10B.

Analysis

The improvements are modest but consistent across scales, supporting the view that PIT acts primarily as a stabilizing inductive bias. In teacher-mode, gains may shrink when the starting checkpoint already has a relatively well-behaved token interface, so improvements show up more strongly in stability diagnostics and post-training behavior than in raw training loss.
5.4 Results on Loss dynamics

We track training loss and perplexity as a function of tokens seen and compare optimization speed at fixed token budgets. Beyond loss dynamics, we report general-purpose evaluation immediately after pretraining to test whether interface stabilization translates into better downstream readiness. We focus on lightweight evaluations that are inexpensive relative to pretraining, including held-out perplexity on a validation shard and zero-shot accuracy on a small suite of standard tasks.

Figure 4 shows representative pretraining loss curves on FineWeb-Edu 10B. The comparison highlights two regimes. In scratch-mode, TT and PIT both train stably, with TT remaining lower across most of training in this particular run. In teacher-mode continued pretraining, PIT is more stable early on, while TT exhibits a brief loss increase that is consistent with an interface mismatch being amplified by large early gradients.
Analysis

Taken together, the curves suggest that PIT mainly reduces optimization friction that originates at the token interface. This effect is easiest to see when the model begins from a state where input-side and output-side token meanings are not well synchronized, which can happen during continued pretraining if the original checkpoint relied on transpose tying and accumulated drift. When starting from scratch, the advantage of PIT is less about dramatic loss improvements and more about keeping the geometry of the token interface stable so that later training and adaptation behave predictably.
5.5 Results On Token-Interface Consistency
We next measure interface consistency directly. Given an embedding EE and an unembedding WoutW_{\text{out}}, a natural scalar diagnostic is the deviation from a left-inverse condition
ΔTI=∥Wout​E−Id∥F,\Delta_{\text{TI}}\;=\;\lVert W_{\text{out}}E-I_{d}\rVert_{F}, (14)
where smaller is better and 00 indicates a perfectly consistent token interface.

Let Bin,Bout∈ℝV×dB_{\text{in}},B_{\text{out}}\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times d} denote input-side and output-side semantic bases. For standard models, we extract them as the orthonormal factors from thin polar decompositions of the embedding matrix and the transposed unembedding matrix, computed in FP32. For PIT, BinB_{\text{in}} and BoutB_{\text{out}} coincide with the shared orthonormal memory ZZ by construction up to numerical precision. We compare BinB_{\text{in}} and BoutB_{\text{out}} using three metrics, each with 00 meaning perfect agreement. We report cosine distance, Procrustes error, and principal angle.
Table 2 reports input-side vs. output-side semantic alignment. PIT reduces all alignment errors to near numerical precision, consistent with the shared-memory construction.

Analysis

These diagnostics capture PIT’s intended effect, keeping the token interface synchronized so that input-side and output-side semantics coincide. In practice, TT drift can evolve during training, so reporting alignment metrics provides a deterministic complement to loss curves and helps interpret post-training update behavior.
5.6 Results on LM Post-Training

We evaluate lightweight adaptation using LoRA (Hu et al., 2022). We fine-tune on MBPP (Austin et al., 2021) for code and GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) for math, then evaluate out-of-domain transfer on HumanEval (Chen, 2021) for code and SVAMP (Patel et al., 2021) for math. We report exact-match accuracy.

To keep the comparison controlled, we use the same LoRA configuration across methods at each scale. The key hypothesis is not that PIT changes what the model can ultimately represent, but that a more consistent token interface makes small, low-rank updates easier to apply without inducing unintended shifts in how hidden states are read out as tokens. This should matter most for transfer, where robustness to distribution shift is often limited by brittle reliance on a particular decoding geometry.

Mode-Model Method MBPP ↑\uparrow HumanEval ↑\uparrow GSM8K ↑\uparrow SVAMP ↑\uparrow Teacher GPT-256M TT 18.7 10.3 16.9 12.4 PIT 19.5 11.6 17.3 13.5 Teacher GPT-590M TT 28.9 19.6 25.7 20.8 PIT 29.3 19.2 26.1 21.5 Teacher GPT-1.3B TT 39.5 29.8 36.2 31.1 PIT 39.9 30.9 36.7 32.3 Scratch Llama-303M TT 16.2 8.7 13.5 10.1 PIT 15.6 8.2 13.1 9.6 Scratch Llama-613M TT 24.8 15.9 21.1 17.0 PIT 24.2 15.4 20.6 16.6 Scratch Llama-1.17B TT 33.6 24.1 31.0 26.4 PIT 32.9 23.6 30.4 25.8
Analysis

The update results are mixed, and the pattern differs by training regime. In teacher-mode, PIT is modestly better in most cells, with the largest gains appearing on harder transfer settings such as HumanEval and SVAMP. This is consistent with the idea that, when starting from a pretrained checkpoint, stabilizing how hidden states map back to vocabulary items can make low-rank updates less brittle and reduce unintended shifts in decoding behavior. In scratch-mode, TT is slightly better across the board in this set of runs. A plausible explanation is that, for these scratch checkpoints, the LoRA adaptation benefits more from the extra degrees of freedom implicit in transpose tying, while PIT’s stricter interface constraint can mildly limit how the update reshapes the token readout. Overall, PIT looks most useful as a safety and robustness bias for continued training and lightweight updates on pretrained models, rather than as a universally dominant choice for scratch models.
